artifact_schema.description: Two messages of equal length, both beginning with the pinned 64-byte prefix, as lowercase hex. The example's m is the prefix followed by one byte, so the prefix every submission has to carry is readable straight off this record.

m.description: The first message, lowercase hex, an even number of characters, at most 8192 of them.

m_prime.description: The second message, same length as m and different from it.

statement: Find a colliding pair for SHA-1 reduced to its first 64 steps (the last 16 are not run; the reduced function is defined by the pinned checker and by nothing else) from a chaining value nobody chose. Both messages must begin with the same pinned 64-byte prefix -- exactly one message block for this function -- must have the same length, must differ somewhere, and must agree on all 160 digest bits. The prefix is sha512("cairn hash-differential v1 sha1-64"), so it is re-derivable by anyone and was chosen by nobody: a funder who picks a prefix can pick one whose chaining value they have already collided, and that is the self-dealing row in docs/threat-model.md. Deriving it also puts every published collision for SHA-1 out of reach as a copy, since all of them start from the standard IV behind a prefix their own author chose. Equal length is required because a same-length collision composes -- H(m || x) = H(m' || x) for every x -- and that is the property worth paying for. Messages are at most 4096 bytes and travel as lowercase hex in {"m", "m_prime"}. This is the bridge rung. Full SHA-0 and full SHA-1 are nearly thirty bits of work apart, and 64-step collisions were found in 2006 at a cost one machine can still pay -- which is where the interesting path engineering sits.
